role: CNC lathe operator (setup technician) at a precision parts factory
headline: A CNC lathe operator four years out of technical school, working alternating day and night shifts at a precision parts factory in Suzhou, minding six Swiss-type lathes, holding a senior-worker certificate and going for CNC lathe technician
unit: A precision machining factory in Xiangcheng, Suzhou, making parts for cars and medical devices
level: You can read a drawing, fixture a part, set tools and tune a Swiss-type lathe on your own, and you usually hold a five-micron tolerance on the first try. Hand-writing macro programs still trips you up, and in CAM you can only edit what your master wrote
intro: You came straight from technical school to this factory and worked your way up from loading parts to tuning a Swiss-type lathe on your own. The shop floor has more than twenty machines that never stop, and six of them are yours, one week on days, one week on nights. As of today, in the gaps between shifts, you are going to earn the CNC lathe technician certificate.
salary_note: Estimate: on alternating shifts at a Suzhou precision machining plant, with night-shift allowances and overtime, take-home pay runs 20-30% above the national figure. In months when orders are thin there is only base pay, and you drop back to the national figure.

facts.label: CNC Setup Technician (current level)
facts.value: 1-3 years, ¥12,500–18,300 a month (at this employer, estimated)

facts.label: What AI can't take
facts.value: Adjusting tool offsets from the CMM report and cutting the first article

facts.label: Where AI is moving in
facts.value: Hand-writing G-code from a 2D drawing to turn a simple shaft

facts.label: Open positions
facts.value: 22 related job listings nationwide, 0 in this city (the listings are mostly graduate hiring and internships)

day: Shift change. The night-shift man from your home province runs through the six machines: the tool tip on number three is worn, and the bone screws on number five started drifting oversize in the small hours. You sign the handover book.
Start-up checks: oil level, air pressure, coolant concentration. You put a drop on the refractometer, the reading is low, and you top it up with half a bucket of concentrate.

Changeover. The new batch is tiny titanium screws for medical devices, less than a millimeter across at the thinnest point. You fit the guide bushing, set the tools, and watch the first bar slowly feed out of the machine.
First article to inspection. The CMM room says the thread pitch diameter is three hundredths of a millimeter off. You go back, change the tool offset, make the trip again, and the second one passes.

The canteen's ¥12 set meal: two meat dishes and a vegetable. You eat while working through practice questions for the technician exam. The old hand across the table says you forget all that once the exam's over; what's in your hands is what's yours.

The shop floor smells of oil mist and coolant, and a row of machines hums in your ears. Every so often you take a part and check it with a micrometer, while your ears listen for the machine that sounds wrong.
Number four stops on an alarm: the chip conveyor has jammed. You shut the door, kill the power and dig out the swarf. Your glove is wound into a knot and your forearm gets a scratch.

You ride your e-bike back to the dormitory past a row of factories with their lights still on. You rinse off, lie down on the top bunk, and scroll through a macro program your master sent, until you fall asleep.

ladder.title: CNC Operator
ladder.focus: Follow shop safety rules to the letter, fixture parts, find centers and set tools, and do basic daily maintenance. Avoid crashing the machine and keep batch tolerances consistently within spec.

ladder.title: CNC Setup Technician
ladder.focus: Read complex drawings and handle fixturing and alignment, regrind tools and fine-tune macro programs on your own. Work with the programmer on first-article cuts, dimensional corrections and troubleshooting on the floor, with the basics of writing and running your own programs.

ladder.title: CNC Programming Engineer
ladder.focus: Step back from running machines and work from the technical office, using CAM software to plan three- and four-axis toolpaths and fixturing. Optimize cutting parameters to deal with tool wear and thermal distortion, and lead sampling and the move into volume production.

ladder.title: Five-Axis CNC Machining Technician
ladder.focus: Take on the hardest five-axis and mill-turn parts for aerospace, medical and precision molds. Master the machine's RTCP and VERICUT collision simulation, write standard process plans, and pass the craft on to apprentices.

ai_tasks.name: Adjusting tool offsets from the CMM report and cutting the first article
ai_tasks.how: AI can help calculate offsets and compare against past parameters. But the first cut means standing at the machine watching the chips, listening and keeping it safe, and when an aerospace part goes wrong, whoever signed answers for it. Only a person can do that.

ai_tasks.name: Hand-writing G-code from a 2D drawing to turn a simple shaft
ai_tasks.how: AI can generate G-code for stepped and threaded shafts straight from the drawing and explain every line. But at this stage the point is to build the basics, so a newcomer writes it by hand, understands it, checks it and has a mentor sign off. AI is just the answer key and the sparring partner.

ai_tasks.name: Programming three-axis roughing for a thin-walled aerospace frame in UG NX and posting the NC program
ai_tasks.how: AI and the CAM software's automatic feature recognition can draft the roughing toolpaths and parameters and help check for collisions in simulation. A person judges the fixturing, the risk of thin walls distorting and the stock allowance, and approves the program before it runs.

ai_tasks.name: Handling a sudden A-axis servo overload alarm while machining a five-axis impeller, and getting back into production
ai_tasks.how: AI can pull up the manual by alarm code and list the usual causes, like a loose fixture or mismatched parameters. But finding the real cause on the spot, checking fixture and spindle, deciding whether to carry on, and whether to risk it to save an expensive part, takes experience and responsibility. Only a person can make that call.

ai_tasks.name: Compensating the finishing process for a mold insert from a full CMM report
ai_tasks.how: AI can read the CMM report, find what's out of tolerance, work out offset corrections and help generate optimized toolpaths in CAM. A person decides whether the error comes from tool wear, heat or fixturing, chooses the compensation, and verifies the result.

ai_tasks.name: Leading five-axis process development and first-article approval for a new titanium aerospace fitting
ai_tasks.how: AI can look up titanium cutting data, help with simulation and organize the process documents. But TC4 is hard to machine, and the choices on compound-angle holes and freeform surfaces, the problems that come up in trial cuts, and the talking and signing through first-article approval all need a person in charge.

events.e_master_ear: Your master walked past behind you, stopped and said: number five sounds dull, the tool needs changing. You didn't believe him. You took it out and the edge had a tiny chip. From that day you started learning to listen to the machines.
events.e_crash: Setting up a new program you missed one tool offset, and the turret slammed into the chuck. The bang made the whole floor turn around. The machine took three days to fix. Your team leader didn't shout; he just had you tape the scrap report to your tool cabinet door.
events.e_first_pass: A batch of medical bone screws, every one right first time from the first article to the last. When the customer came to audit the plant, they leafed through your inspection records and nodded.
events.e_night: A full week of nights, and three in the morning is the hardest. You dozed off on your feet and the alarm jolted you awake, your heart pounding.
events.e_rush: A car customer's order was rushed, and the floor went two months without a day off. The overtime on your pay slip was more than your base pay, and you sent a chunk of it home.
events.e_love: A girl from the electronics factory next door ate at the same barbecue stall every night. You swapped WeChat contacts, and she said you always smelled of machine oil, but not in a bad way.
events.e_dermatitis: A red rash broke out on the backs of your hands and itched so badly you couldn't sleep. The factory doctor said it was a coolant allergy. You switched to nitrile gloves, and in summer they filled with sweat.
events.e_mes: The factory networked its machines, and every one's uptime, alarms and output now hang on a big screen over the floor. Whose machine has been idle longest, anyone can see at a glance.
events.e_contest: You represented the factory in the district's CNC lathe skills contest and took second prize, ¥3,000. They hung a banner over the factory gate, with one character of your name printed wrong.
events.e_wedding: You held the wedding back home in Henan, and the bride price and the banquet used up several years of overtime pay. On the day, the bridesmaids laughed at the calluses on your hands for ages.
events.e_japan_audit: A Japanese customer came to audit. An old engineer crouched by your machine for half an hour, then pointed at your gauge log and said something. The interpreter said: he says it's very clean.
events.e_slump: Orders thinned out, the floor went on rotating days off, four days a week. Someone in the dormitory packed his bags for Kunshan, saying a factory there was hiring.
events.e_baby: When the baby came you were on nights for a stretch, and spent the days at the hospital. A nurse showed you how to trim the baby's nails. You said, I make parts to five microns, my hands are steady.
events.e_robot_arm: The shop installed robot arms for automatic loading and unloading, and one person went from minding six machines to twelve. The job of standing by a machine feeding it was gone; what's left is setup, changeovers and alarms.
events.e_ai_gcode: The technical office tried out AI programming: one look at a drawing and it spits out G-code. You ran it in simulation and the first block crashed into the part, and it took you a long time to make it usable. You were relieved, and a little uneasy.
events.e_house: You bought a small two-bedroom flat in the north of Suzhou, the down payment pooled from both families, so that one day your child could earn the residence points to go to school here. With the mortgage on your back, you never turned down a night shift again.
events.e_apprentice: Your apprentice passed his intermediate-grade certificate and treated you to barbecue outside the factory gate. He said, Master, that line of yours, “listen first, then measure,” I saved it in my phone notes.
events.e_back: Years of standing and bending over parts, and your lower back was the first to go. Squatting down to fixture a part, you have to hold on to the machine to get up.
events.e_relocate: The boss said he'd open a branch plant in Anhui and move some of Suzhou's orders there. The floor was on edge, and some people had already gone to ask what the branch would pay.
events.e_father: A call from home: your father fell in the fields and has a compression fracture in his spine. You took a week off to go back, and that month's pay came up badly short.
events.e_young: The shop couldn't hire young people this year; everyone who came was in their forties. You went to a technical school to recruit, and the first question from the students was: is the shop air-conditioned?
events.e_ears: At the checkup the hearing test showed amber. Twenty-odd machines have roared beside you for more than ten years, and now you raise your voice without noticing when you talk.

c_tech.title: Go for the CNC lathe technician certificate
c_tech.situation: The factory gets two places a year to apply for technician. You hand in a technical report, pass a theory exam and a practical, then defend it before a panel. The only time to prepare is the day after a night shift, which is exactly when you sleep.

options.label: Apply, and practice after nights
options.result: You slept four or five hours and went to the training workshop, and spent three months grinding through macro programs. At the defense a judge asked about cutting threads, and you answered with the time you crashed the machine.

options.label: Not yet, save some money
options.result: The place went to someone else. You took more overtime, and the number on your bank card looked a little better. Your master glanced at you and said nothing.

c_cam.title: Move to the technical office and learn CAM programming
c_cam.situation: The technical office needs someone who can program in UG, and the supervisor asks if you'll come over, starting from drawing toolpaths, on the way to CNC Programming Engineer. No more night shifts, but for the first year you'd earn over a thousand less than on the floor, with no overtime.

options.label: Go to the technical office
options.result: You went from standing to sitting, from watching the tool tip to watching toolpaths on a screen. The first time a program you wrote ran on a machine, you stood beside it for an hour without leaving.

options.label: Stay by the machines
options.result: You said you wanted a few more years with your hands on the machines. Whenever anyone's machine won't run right they call you, your hands get steadier, and the overtime on your pay slip stays the same.

c_kunshan.title: Jump to a foreign-owned plant in Kunshan to learn five-axis
c_kunshan.situation: A classmate from technical school works at a foreign-owned precision plant in Kunshan. They've brought in a row of five-axis machining centers, they're short of people, the pay is thirty percent higher, three shifts. You'd learn five-axis from scratch, and start your social insurance over there.

options.label: Go to Kunshan
options.result: You got your hands on a five-axis machine for the first time and crashed into the fixture twice in the first month. The money really was better, and three shifts took your sleep apart.

options.label: Stay in Suzhou
options.result: You stayed, and the factory gave you a ¥500 raise. Your classmate sent a photo of a five-axis impeller, and you zoomed in on it for a long time.

c_ai_cam.title: Learn AI programming and simulation, or not
c_ai_cam.situation: The technical office has brought in an AI programming assistant that recognizes features and generates toolpaths on its own. The supervisor wants someone to review the programs it writes, and turn the shop floor's experience into rules to feed it. Some say that's teaching the machine to take your job.

options.label: Learn it, review its programs
options.result: You became the best person on the floor at catching the AI's mistakes: which feed is too aggressive, where a thin wall will warp, you can see it at a glance. The supervisor started bringing you to meetings.

options.label: Don't, let the hands do the talking
options.result: You still write your own programs and do your own trial cuts. The AI writes more and more programs, and when something goes wrong, people still come to you.

c_five_axis.title: Lead the five-axis push, aim for Five-Axis CNC Machining Technician
c_five_axis.situation: The factory has an order for titanium aerospace fittings that needs simultaneous five-axis work, and nobody dares to commit. The boss asks if you'll lead it. Pull it off, and you have a claim to Five-Axis CNC Machining Technician; get it wrong, and each blank costs thousands.

options.label: Take it, lead the project
options.result: You lived in the simulation software for a month, scrapped four blanks, and the fifth passed first-article approval. The boss read your name out at the all-hands meeting.

options.label: Leave it to an outside expert
options.result: The factory paid for a five-axis specialist from outside. You followed him around for six months and filled a notebook.

c_hometown.title: Go back to the branch plant in Anhui
c_hometown.situation: The boss has opened the branch in Anhui and wants you there as a technical lead, for twenty percent less pay, an hour's drive from your hometown. Your child goes to school back home, and you see them only a few times a year.

options.label: Go to the branch
options.result: You could go home every weekend now. The branch's machines are a bit older than Suzhou's, and your apprentices are kids fresh out of school.

options.label: Stay in Suzhou
options.result: You stayed. On the video call every night your child asks when you're coming home, and you say once this batch ships.

c_supervisor.title: Become shop supervisor, or stay technical
c_supervisor.situation: The shop supervisor has been transferred, and the plant manager wants you to take over: scheduling, uptime and safety for more than thirty people. You know that once you take it, you'll rarely touch a machine again.

options.label: Take the supervisor job
options.result: You started planning production, running morning meetings, approving leave and breaking up arguments, with uptime chasing you at the end of every month. The last time you set a tool yourself was two months ago.

options.label: Stay technical
options.result: You turned it down and someone else got it. Every time he hits a hard part, the first call he makes is to you.

c_app_eng.title: Go to a machine-tool maker as an applications engineer
c_app_eng.situation: A machine-tool company sent someone to commission new equipment on your floor, and he watched you get their machine running smoothly in a few moves. He asks if you'd join them as an applications engineer: visiting customers all over the country, running trial cuts, teaching people to use the machines, and no shifts.

options.label: Join the machine-tool maker
options.result: You boarded the high-speed train with a case of tools and gauges.
options.end: You spend most of the year on the road, tuning machines for people in one strange shop after another, teaching young operators to listen first, then measure.

options.label: Stay at the factory
options.result: You said no; the machines here couldn't do without you. He left a business card, and you tucked it into the operating manual.

c_own_shop.title: Go into a small machining shop with a friend from home
c_own_shop.situation: A man from your hometown has rented a small unit in Xiangcheng, bought three secondhand CNC lathes and is taking subcontract work. He wants you to buy in and run the technical side. It takes a big chunk of money; when work comes there's no day or night, and when it doesn't, you wait.

options.label: Buy in
options.result: You put in most of your savings.
options.end: In a sheet-metal shed you chase customers and quote prices by day, and set up the machines yourself at night. You could tell those three secondhand lathes apart by sound with your eyes shut.

options.label: Stay on wages
options.result: You kept your money. Two years later his shop had grown to eight machines, and one year it nearly closed. He took you to dinner and talked all night.

endings.retire: On your last shift you wipe down the machine you've tuned for more than ten years, oil the guideways, mix the coolant just right. In the handover book you write the last line: number five sounds normal. As you walk out the gate, the night shift is coming in, and they nod to you.
endings.burnout: That day you crouched to fixture a part and your back wouldn't straighten, and you sat on the floor for half an hour. The factory doctor wrote you a sick note, and the shop moved you to the stores to look after the tooling. You leave on time every day, and when you pass the shop floor you still stop for a moment to listen.

past: You missed the cutoff for academic high school by more than thirty points. Your father, who farms back in Henan, said learning a trade at technical school beat drifting through high school. The recruiter said CNC was easy to find work in; the factories in Suzhou were fighting over people.
You followed someone from your village to a technical school in Suzhou and joined the CNC class. The whole first year was drawings and benchwork, and you spent a month filing one square block.

The first time on a manual lathe, the teacher had you turn a steel bar to the drawing. You took off two hundredths of a millimeter too much and scrapped the whole bar. That day you learned what a hundredth of a millimeter is.

You passed the intermediate-grade CNC lathe certificate and were placed at this precision plant on an internship, starting with loading, deburring and measuring. Half your class went to electronics assembly lines, saying at least there was no swarf.
You finished the senior-worker program with the senior-grade certificate and stayed on at the plant where you'd interned. Your first month's pay was just over ¥4,000, and you sent half of it home.

Your master started leaving two Swiss-type lathes to you alone. Once you spent a whole night tuning by yourself, and when the first good bone screw came out in the morning, you held it in your fingers and looked at it for a long time.

late.pension_note: Estimate: Suzhou's basic pension for company employees, with a contribution base that rose and fell with overtime pay, comes to a little over forty percent of your final monthly pay. There is no company annuity.
scenes: For the first month of retirement you still wake on the hour, and the moment you wake your ears prick up. The quiet in the flat feels strange.
A small factory nearby asks you to help with setups two days a week: read drawings, set tools, teach. You say you don't want money, and the owner presses two cartons of cigarettes on you.
Your child finished school in Suzhou and joined a company that makes robots. He says their machines use the kind of tiny parts you used to make, and you ask him what the tolerance is.
Downstairs you fix a neighbor's child's bicycle, a stripped screw that you clean up with a file. The neighbor says you're good with your hands. You say you did this all your life.
You hand out tooling in the stores, booking things in and out by the slip. Your back no longer aches at night and you sleep straight through, on a smaller wage.

A young machinist comes for tools and says a batch keeps drifting on size. You ask a couple of questions about how the machine sounds and tell him to check the spindle temperature. He leaves half convinced, and comes back in the afternoon to say you were right.
When the time came you retired, went back to Henan for a while, then came back to Suzhou. Your child is here, and you say home is wherever your child is.
In the first year away from that shop floor you kept waking in the night, thinking one of the machines was alarming.

You found your feet in the new place. When you go back to the old factory on errands, your former apprentice walks you round the floor. You listen your way down the row and say number three is due for maintenance.
One of the people you trained became a five-axis technician. The day he was certified he called you, and the first thing he said was: Master, I listened first.

Later there were more and more machines on the floor and fewer and fewer people, and the numbers on the big screen never stopped. But when a machine sounded wrong, someone still had to walk over and listen.
You have a few old scars on your fingers from swarf. Your grandson touches them and asks if they hurt. You say not anymore; they're marks from making parts.

closing.retire: Many years later, waiting for a prescription at the hospital, you see a photo of an orthopedic implant on the notice board, and you recognize the thread on that little screw at once. You stand looking at it for a long time, until they call your number.
closing.burnout: Many years later, on the balcony, you measure your grandson's building-block pieces with an old caliper and tell him they're very accurately made. He doesn't understand, and you don't explain. You wipe the caliper clean and put it back in its box.
closing.end: Many years later you find your technical school workshop manual in a drawer. The first page records the measurements of that filed square block, in crooked handwriting. You look at it for a while, then put it back.

stages: You are the one between the operators and the technical office. When a programmer sends a program, you dry-run it and single-block the first cut; which feed is too aggressive, which tool can't reach, you write on the back of the process sheet and send it back. When an operator hits an alarm you're the first one they shout for, and you have to say clearly what can keep running and what must stop. People on the floor have started calling you Master.

You've moved into the technical office, with two screens on the desk, one running UG, one running VERICUT. Every day you program toolpaths for new parts, run collision simulations, post NC programs and process cards, then go down to the floor to watch the first part run. You argue with quality over a tolerance and with purchasing over the price of a box of imported inserts. The lines you draw, others run on the machines.

You take the parts nobody else will touch: titanium fittings, impellers, thin-walled frames. By day you watch RTCP and the tool axis at the five-axis machine; at night you tune post-processors in simulation; when a customer's engineers audit the process, you answer them point by point. You train apprentices and write standard process plans, and a program you've signed carries your name.
work: A new operator knocked the tool setter out of line and scrambled the offsets on three machines. You recalibrated each one with a reference bar and had them running again by midnight.
A programmer sent a mill-turn program. Single-blocking it on the machine, at line forty you saw the live tool would hit the tailstock, circled it in red and sent it back.
An inspector brought you a CMM report: a batch of valve spools was two microns out of round. You fitted a new set of soft jaws, and the next batch all passed.
In UG you programmed three-axis roughing for a car bracket, ran it through VERICUT, and found the toolholder would graze a clamp. You moved it five millimeters.
The purchasing manager brought a quote for imported inserts and asked if domestic ones would do. You cut fifty parts with each and wrote on the comparison sheet: not for finishing.
An old operator complained your programs were too timid. You spread the cutting-data table in front of him and explained, line by line, why a thin wall can't take a cut that deep.

The customer's quality engineer went through a stack of process documents, asking page by page about your fixturing for the five-axis impeller. You answered all afternoon, and he signed the audit sheet.
In Post Builder you revised the post-processor for the new five-axis machine. Your apprentice watched all day, and in the end found a small mistake himself.
The plant manager brought a shortlist for new equipment and asked whether to buy another mill-turn center. You went through six months of orders and said: not yet.
